facts.statement: Charles Gilmore originally described the remains as a new species of Pteranodon in 1928.
facts.quote: In 1928, Charles Gilmore named a new species of Pteranodon: P. oregonensis.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a humerus, two fused dorsal vertebrae, and a fragment of a joint bone found in the Albian stage of the Hudspeth Formation in Oregon.
facts.quote: A humerus (holotype MPUC V.126713), two fused dorsal vertebrae and the broken-off end of some joint bone had been unearthed from the Lower Cretaceous (Albian stage) beds of the Hudspeth Formation in Wheeler County, Oregon, United States

facts.statement: Lev Nessov established the genus Bennettazhia in 1991 after reclassifying the remains from a pteranodontid to an azhdarchid.
facts.quote: In 1991, Russian paleontologist Lev Nessov therefore named a new azhdarchid genus: Bennettazhia.

facts.statement: S. Christopher Bennett later changed his classification in 1994, suggesting the genus belonged to the Dsungaripteridae.
facts.quote: Bennett himself in 1994 changed his opinion and stated that it belonged to the Dsungaripteridae.

facts.statement: Evidence of guano and fragmented ammonites suggests Bennettazhia ate molluscs and lived in large colonies on cliffs.
facts.quote: In 2023, the discovery of guano and unusual fragmentation of ammonites from the Hudspeth Formation have been interpreted as evidence that this pterosaur ate molluscs and formed large colonies on nearby cliffs similar to modern seagull rookeries.

facts.statement: In 2025, researchers noted that new remains attributed to Bennettazhia showed no overlap with the original holotype.
facts.quote: However, in 2025, it was noted that these remains were referred to Bennettazhia without any overlap with the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: Bennettazhia lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Oregon, United States.
facts.quote: Bennettazhia is a genus of tapejaromorph pterosaur which lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous from what is now the Hudspeth Formation of the state of Oregon in the United States.

facts.statement: The 183 mm long humerus of the holotype is uncrushed, providing a rare opportunity to study its internal structure.
facts.quote: The humerus, 183 mm long, is uncrushed, which is uncommon for a pterosaur fossil and therefore offered a rare opportunity to investigate the bone structure.

facts.statement: The humerus featured a thin outer wall filled with spongy tissue made of trabeculae and struts, creating a light but strong structure.
facts.quote: Apart from the thin bone wall, the humerus was filled with a spongy tissue consisting of trabeculae, very thin bone layers and struts, forming a light yet strong construction.

facts.statement: The humerus possesses an elongated, unwarped deltopectoral crest.
facts.quote: The humerus has an elongated deltopectoral crest that is unwarped.

facts.statement: Michael Habib concluded that Bennettazhia belongs to the Azhdarchoidea, a broader group than the Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: Habib concluded that Bennettazhia was a member of the Azhdarchoidea, a more encompassing group than the Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: Bennett later established that the genus belonged to the family Dsungaripteridae.
facts.quote: El propio Bennett cambió su opinión y estableció que el género pertenecía a la familia Dsungaripteridae.

facts.statement: Several authors classified Bennettazhia as a Pterodactyloidea of uncertain affinity (incertae sedis) for many years.
facts.quote: Wellnhofer (1991), Peters (1997), Kellner (2003) y Unwin (2003) se limitaron a establecerlo como un Pterodactyloidea incertae sedis.

facts.statement: Bennettazhia lived between 113.2 and 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (113.2 to 100.5 million years ago)
